title: Knowledge check — 8 questions
note: Unlocks after the applied activity is submitted. Retakes are free and unlimited.

questions.prompt: What is the test the module gives for whether your effective dating actually works?
options: Whether every record has a start date populated
Whether the system can answer who this person's manager was on a specific date last year — not just who it is now
Whether historical records are archived rather than deleted
Whether date fields are validated on entry
questions.explanation: Most systems answer the present-tense question instantly and cannot answer the historical one, or answer it wrongly because a correction was applied without a date. Every trend and cohort analysis depends on the second answer.

questions.prompt: What does "a field being populated is not a field being true" mean for data-quality metrics?
options: That completeness statistics should be weighted by field importance
That every metric you have been shown measures completeness — which is easy to measure and easy to fake with a default value — while nobody measures truth
That populated fields should be audited annually
That required fields produce better data than optional ones
questions.explanation: And it is the reason the number in Lesson 2 does not exist. You can populate a field in an afternoon; you cannot make it true in an afternoon.

questions.prompt: Why does this module have no anchor statistic? `[V]`
options: Because HR data quality varies too much between organizations to benchmark
Because the relevant figures are held privately by HCM vendors

Because no credible measurement exists — the available figures trace to vendor blogs citing each other, an undisclosed-sample vendor survey, consultancy claims with no methodology, and an unattributed anecdote
Because the module is argued from craft rather than evidence by design
questions.explanation: A course that teaches you to ask "what's the sample?" has to answer it about its own evidence. Building the lesson on the undisclosed-sample figure would have been the exact failure this curriculum spends eight modules warning about.

questions.prompt: How does the module turn that absence into an argument?
options: By arguing that unmeasurable problems are usually overstated
Because work nobody measures is work nobody funds, and unfunded unowned work generates no research — so the missing number is a symptom of the condition the module is about
By substituting qualitative evidence for quantitative
By deferring the question to the People Analytics track
questions.explanation: If data quality were funded, measured and owned, there would be benchmarks. There are none, and that is informative rather than merely inconvenient.

questions.prompt: What is the significance of the payroll error survey in this lesson? `[V]`
options: It measures HR data quality directly
It shows the cause is unmeasured while the downstream symptom has a disclosed-sample number — which is why you build the business case on the symptom
It proves that payroll systems are less reliable than HR systems
It provides the cost figure to use in any remediation business case
questions.explanation: Roughly one in five US payrolls containing errors, from 508 practitioners at companies of 250–10,000 employees, 2022. Consultancy survey, four years old, modelled per-error cost — and its sample is disclosed, which is the comparison that matters. D over-claims: use your own measured symptom, not this figure.

questions.prompt: Why is data-quality work described as unambiguously safe AI work?
options: Because it involves no employee-identifying data
Because it makes no decisions about people — it finds where the record disagrees with itself — and every candidate finding is independently checkable in seconds
Because errors in it are self-correcting over time
Because it operates on aggregate rather than individual records
questions.explanation: The checkability is what makes it safe rather than merely useful: you do not have to trust the model, you open the row. That is a different risk posture from everything else in the track. A is false — it works on exactly that data.

questions.prompt: Why does the four-line business case work when "we need better data" does not?
options: Because it quantifies the total cost of poor data quality
Because it is shorter and executives prefer brevity
Because it reframes the ask from a new project competing for funding into a prerequisite for something leadership has already promised in public
Because it assigns the work to another function's budget
questions.explanation: A request gets weighed against other requests. A risk to something already committed is a different conversation with a different default — and you are the only person who can see it.

questions.prompt: Why is a bulk correction itself a dangerous change?
options: Because bulk updates bypass field-level validation

Because it is a wide-reach long-latency change by construction, so a remediation run badly is indistinguishable from the problem it fixed — and it is made under time pressure by someone embarrassed about the original
Because correction scripts cannot be version-controlled
Because vendors do not support bulk operations on all fields
questions.explanation: Which is why the form is a candidate list with a reason per row, a real sample looking for *families* of false positive, batches small enough to reverse, and a reconciliation of the changed count against the approved count.
